Age: 40  
Sex: Female  
Complaint: Persistent nasal congestion, frequent sneezing, and clear rhinorrhea for 2 years, worsening with dusting/vacuuming; no asthma, wheezing, or shortness of breath.  

Analysis: All three experts unanimously identified the presentation as chronic/perennial allergic rhinitis based on year‑round watery rhinorrhea, pale boggy mucosa, transverse nasal crease (allergic salute), and symptom provocation by dust exposure. Consensus was reached that there are no red‑flag features (fever, purulent discharge, facial pain, epistaxis, visual changes, lower‑airway involvement), so urgent evaluation is unnecessary. First‑line pharmacologic management (daily intranasal corticosteroid spray, second‑generation oral antihistamine, isotonic saline irrigation) and avoidance of prolonged topical decongestant use were agreed upon. Environmental control focusing on dust‑mite reduction, and elective allergy testing (skin‑prick or serum‑specific IgE) were also uniformly endorsed. Referral to ENT after 4–6 weeks of optimal therapy or if structural pathology is suspected, and referral to allergy/immunology for detailed testing or immunotherapy, were agreed upon. Screening for atopic comorbidities (asthma, AERD, atopic dermatitis, allergic conjunctivitis) and for hormonal or occupational triggers was recommended by all. Long‑term management includes maintenance intranasal steroids, PRN antihistamines, and consideration of immunotherapy if symptoms persist.

Points of minor divergence: One expert explicitly emphasized screening for asthma/AERD, whereas the others mentioned asthma screening but not AERD. Only one expert highlighted the risk of rhinitis medicamentosa from topical decongestants, though the others warned against prolonged use. Resource adequacy ratings varied (8–10), reflecting slight differences in perceived need for imaging or specialist resources. Additional considerations raised outside the core consensus included evaluation for mold, indoor tobacco smoke, family history of atopy, and monitoring for progression to chronic rhinosinusitis or otitis media.

Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Skin‑prick testing or serum‑specific IgE assay for dust‑mite and other indoor allergens; nasal endoscopy or sinus CT scan only if symptoms persist despite maximal medical therapy or if structural abnormality is suspected; pulmonary function testing (spirometry) if asthma symptoms develop; basic otoscopic examination to screen for middle‑ear effusion.  

Conclusion: Chronic/perennial allergic rhinitis, likely driven by dust‑mite exposure, without red‑flag features.  

Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care  
Subclinical specialization: Otolaryngology (ENT)  

Recommendations: Initiate daily intranasal corticosteroid spray combined with a second‑generation oral antihistamine and isotonic saline irrigation; avoid topical decongestant sprays longer than 3–5 days to prevent rhinitis medicamentosa. Implement comprehensive dust‑mite control: allergen‑proof mattress and pillow encasements, wash bedding weekly in ≥60 °C water, use a HEPA‑filter vacuum, remove or encase carpets, keep indoor humidity below 50 %, and eliminate tobacco smoke and visible mold. Schedule elective skin‑prick or serum‑specific IgE testing to confirm sensitization and guide possible allergen immunotherapy. Obtain a detailed family history of atopy and screen for comorbid asthma, aspirin‑exacerbated respiratory disease, atopic dermatitis, and allergic conjunctivitis; consider baseline spirometry if any wheeze emerges. Assess hormonal status (pregnancy, menstrual cycle, thyroid function) and occupational exposures (cleaning agents, volatile irritants) that may aggravate rhinitis. Counsel the patient on medication side‑effects: monitor for nasal dryness or epistaxis from steroids, sedation or anticholinergic effects from antihistamines, and rebound congestion from decongestants. Arrange follow‑up in 4–6 weeks using a validated rhinitis symptom score to evaluate control, adherence, and adverse effects; if control is inadequate, intensify therapy, reinforce environmental measures, or refer to ENT for possible structural evaluation or to allergy/immunology for immunotherapy. If symptoms do not improve with optimal therapy, reconsider a diagnosis of non‑allergic rhinitis and pursue appropriate work‑up. Monitor longitudinally for progression to chronic rhinosinusitis, otitis media, or sinus complications.  

Notes: The transverse nasal crease supports chronic allergic etiology; family history, mold exposure, and indoor tobacco smoke should be specifically queried.

Age: 16 years  
Sex: Female  
Complaint: Fever, sore throat, difficulty swallowing, fatigue, cervical lymphadenopathy, exudative pharyngitis with soft‑palate petechiae, faint macular rash  

Analysis: The panel converged on Epstein‑Barr virus (EBV) infectious mononucleosis as the most likely diagnosis, citing the classic triad of fever, exudative pharyngitis, and cervical adenopathy together with soft‑palate petechiae and a macular rash in an adolescent. Experts B and C emphasized the need for a focused laboratory work‑up (CBC with differential, heterophile antibody test, EBV serology, rapid streptococcal test, basic metabolic panel, liver enzymes, COVID‑19 test, and CMV serology) to confirm EBV, exclude bacterial pharyngitis, and assess organ involvement. Expert C additionally highlighted the importance of obtaining missing clinical details (splenomegaly, recent antibiotic exposure, exposure history, fever pattern, and red‑flag signs) that were not provided in the vignette. Expert A considered the questionnaire sufficient, an outlier view that was noted but did not alter the diagnostic consensus.  

Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Complete blood count with differential, heterophile antibody (Monospot) test, EBV viral capsid antigen IgM/IgG and EBNA IgG serology if needed, rapid antigen detection test or throat culture for Group A Streptococcus, basic metabolic panel, liver function tests (AST, ALT, bilirubin), SARS‑CoV‑2 PCR or antigen test, cytomegalovirus IgM/IgG serology, and physical examination for splenomegaly and assessment of vital signs.  

Conclusion: The presentation is most consistent with EBV infectious mononucleosis.  

Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care  
Subclinical specialization: Pediatrics  

Recommendations: Obtain a detailed history including recent antibiotic use (especially amoxicillin), travel or exposure to ill contacts, fever pattern, and any abdominal pain that might suggest splenomegaly. Perform a thorough physical exam to assess for splenomegaly and other organomegaly. Order the laboratory panel outlined above; if the heterophile test is negative but suspicion remains high, proceed to EBV serology. Rule out Group A Streptococcus before prescribing antibiotics; avoid amoxicillin if EBV is confirmed, as it can precipitate a rash. Counsel the patient to avoid contact sports or heavy exertion for at least 3–4 weeks or until splenomegaly is excluded, to reduce the risk of splenic rupture. Provide supportive care (adequate hydration, antipyretics, throat lozenges) and arrange follow‑up in 5–7 days or sooner if worsening symptoms, new rash, jaundice, or signs of airway compromise develop.  

Notes: Monitor liver enzymes and complete blood count for trends; consider referral to pediatric infectious disease if atypical features or complications arise.

Age: 4 years  
Sex: Male  
Complaint: Rapidly progressive sore throat, difficulty swallowing, noisy breathing, drooling, tripod positioning, high fever, muffled voice, refusal to speak or drink  

Analysis: All three experts converged on the diagnosis of acute epiglottitis (supraglottitis) based on the classic clinical triad of high fever, toxic appearance, severe drooling, and the thumb sign on lateral neck X‑ray. There was unanimous agreement that the airway can occlude within minutes, mandating emergent, controlled endotracheal intubation by an experienced anesthesia/ENT team while preserving spontaneous ventilation and having surgical airway equipment immediately available. Consensus also existed on immediate supportive measures (upright position, supplemental O₂, large‑bore IV access, avoidance of oropharyngeal manipulation), empiric IV broad‑spectrum antibiotics covering Haemophilus influenzae type b (e.g., ceftriaxone), a single dose of dexamethasone to reduce edema, and the need for ICU admission for close monitoring. No dissenting opinions or alternative approaches were reported among the experts.  

Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Lateral neck X‑ray (thumb sign), continuous pulse‑oximetry, cardiac monitor, large‑bore intravenous access, blood cultures, complete blood count with differential, basic metabolic panel, lactate level, video laryngoscope or fiberoptic scope for controlled intubation, surgical airway set (cricothyrotomy kit, tracheostomy set), supplemental oxygen delivery devices, intravenous ceftriaxone (or cefotaxime), intravenous dexamethasone, fluid resuscitation supplies, pediatric ICU monitoring equipment.  

Conclusion: Acute epiglottitis requiring emergent airway protection and intensive care.  

Emergency type: Requires emergent care  
Subclinical specialization: Pediatrics  

Recommendations: Keep the child upright in the tripod position and minimize agitation; do not perform any oral or pharyngeal examination or manipulation until the airway is secured. Immediately activate a joint anesthesia‑ENT response, transport the patient to the operating room, and prepare for controlled endotracheal intubation while maintaining spontaneous ventilation. Have a surgical airway (cricothyrotomy or tracheostomy) kit ready for immediate use if intubation fails. Begin supplemental oxygen, obtain large‑bore IV access, and start empiric IV ceftriaxone (or cefotaxime) covering Hib; administer a single dose of IV dexamethasone to reduce airway edema. Draw blood cultures, CBC with differential, basic metabolic panel, and lactate before antibiotics if it does not delay therapy. After airway stabilization, admit the patient to a pediatric intensive care unit for at least 24–48 hours of continuous monitoring of respiratory status, oxygenation, hemodynamics, and potential re‑edema. Continue IV antibiotics for 5–7 days, reassess the need for additional steroid dosing, and ensure fluid and electrolyte management. Educate caregivers about the urgency of the situation, the reasons for limited oral intake and examination, and the importance of completing the Hib vaccination series to prevent future episodes.  

Notes: Ensure that all team members are briefed on the need to avoid any manipulation of the oropharynx prior to airway control, and confirm that surgical airway equipment is functional and immediately accessible.

Sex: Male  
Complaint: Persistent low mood, anhedonia, insomnia with early awakening, significant weight loss, difficulty concentrating, feelings of worthlessness, psychomotor retardation, poor grooming, and functional decline over the past 2 months.  

Analysis: All three experts converged on a diagnosis of a single‑episode, severe Major Depressive Disorder (MDD) without psychotic features, supported by DSM‑5 criteria and a PHQ‑9 score of 22. There was unanimous agreement that no immediate safety threats (suicidal ideation, psychosis, severe agitation) are present, leading to the consensus emergency classification of non‑emergent care. Experts A and B emphasized the need for prompt outpatient evaluation and treatment initiation, while Expert C highlighted a broader differential diagnosis—including adjustment disorder, persistent depressive disorder, bipolar depression, and medical conditions such as hypothyroidism—suggesting that these possibilities be actively ruled out. The only point of divergence was the emphasis on differential considerations (Expert C) versus a focus on safety and treatment planning (Experts A and B).  

Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Baseline laboratory panel (complete blood count, comprehensive metabolic panel, thyroid‑stimulating hormone and free T4, vitamin B12, folate, fasting glucose); urine drug screen if substance use is suspected; HIV and syphilis serology if risk factors are present; electrocardiogram if clinically indicated; baseline PHQ‑9 repeat; standardized suicidality assessment (e.g., Columbia‑Suicide Severity Rating Scale); structured psychosocial interview covering family psychiatric history, substance use, medication review, social support, recent stressors, sleep patterns, and trauma history.  

Conclusion: Major Depressive Disorder, severe, single episode, without psychotic features.  

Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care  
Subclinical specialization: Psychiatry  

Recommendations: Initiate first‑line pharmacotherapy with an SSRI (e.g., sertraline 50 mg daily) after confirming no contraindications and reviewing current medications for depressive side‑effects. Arrange referral for evidence‑based psychotherapy such as cognitive‑behavioral therapy or interpersonal therapy. Schedule a follow‑up appointment within 1–2 weeks to assess medication tolerance, side‑effects, and any emergence of suicidal thoughts using a standardized scale. Conduct the comprehensive laboratory work‑up outlined above to exclude medical contributors, especially given the >10 % unintentional weight loss and psychomotor retardation. Obtain a detailed family psychiatric history to screen for mood disorders or bipolar spectrum conditions; if any bipolar features are identified, reconsider antidepressant monotherapy. Screen for current substance use (alcohol, cannabis, stimulants, opioids) and document any recent changes. Review all prescribed and over‑the‑counter medications for depressive side‑effects. Evaluate the patient’s level of social support, recent stressors beyond the breakup, and any history of trauma or abuse; engage supportive contacts as part of the treatment plan. Provide education on sleep hygiene and assess sleep patterns to guide behavioral interventions. Document the severity markers (weight loss, psychomotor retardation, poor grooming) as red flags that warrant close monitoring for potential escalation of suicidality despite current denial. If depressive symptoms do not improve or worsen after an adequate trial (4–6 weeks) of the SSRI, consider augmentation strategies (e.g., atypical antipsychotic, bupropion) or referral to a psychiatrist for possible medication adjustment or higher‑level care.  

Notes: Ensure documentation of informed consent for medication, discuss potential activation syndrome, and provide the patient with crisis resources (e.g., 988 suicide and crisis lifeline).

A 29-year-old male software developer presents with eye fatigue, dryness, and a mild headache that worsens throughout the workday. He spends 10 to 12 hours daily in front of computer screens and often forgets to take breaks. He reports that symptoms improve on weekends when he reduces screen time. Age: 29  
Sex: Male  
Complaint: Eye fatigue, dryness, and a mild headache that worsen throughout prolonged computer work and improve on weekends.  

Analysis: All three experts converged on the diagnosis of digital eye strain (computer vision syndrome) with associated mild dry‑eye symptoms. The history of 10–12 hours of daily screen time, symptom fluctuation with screen exposure, normal visual acuity, intact extraocular movements, reactive pupils, and only mild conjunctival injection support this conclusion. Each expert agreed that no red‑flag findings (e.g., acute glaucoma, uveitis, retinal detachment, optic neuropathy) are present, making the condition non‑urgent. The consensus was uniform; there were no differing opinions on diagnosis, red‑flag assessment, or initial management, although confidence levels reported by the experts varied.  

Required diagnostic equipment/tests: No immediate diagnostic testing is required. If symptoms persist beyond 2–4 weeks, a comprehensive refraction, slit‑lamp examination for dry‑eye evaluation, and assessment for blepharitis or meibomian gland dysfunction should be considered.  

Conclusion: Digital eye strain (computer vision syndrome) with mild ocular surface irritation; self‑limited and amenable to self‑care measures.  

Emergency type: Self-care appropriate  
Subclinical specialization: Ophthalmology  

Recommendations: Implement the 20‑20‑20 rule (every 20 minutes, look at an object 20 feet away for 20 seconds) and schedule regular short breaks from the screen. Optimize workstation ergonomics: position the monitor at eye level, keep a distance of about 50–70 cm, reduce glare with appropriate lighting, and ensure proper posture. Increase conscious blinking and use preservative‑free artificial tears as needed to alleviate dryness. Encourage adequate hydration, limit excessive caffeine, and address psychosocial stressors that may exacerbate symptoms. If symptoms do not improve within 2–4 weeks, obtain a full refraction to rule out uncorrected refractive error and perform a dry‑eye work‑up, including assessment for blepharitis or meibomian gland dysfunction. Should ocular surface disease be identified, initiate targeted therapy (e.g., lid hygiene, warm compresses). Screen for tension‑type headache and consider evaluation for convergence insufficiency or accommodative spasm if the headache persists despite ocular measures. Referral to an ophthalmologist is indicated only if symptoms remain refractory or new concerning signs develop.  

Notes: Mild conjunctival injection is likely secondary to ocular surface irritation from reduced blink rate. The normal fundus and anterior segment examinations reduce the likelihood of serious ocular pathology.

Sex: Female  
Complaint: Shortness of breath and cough of several days’ duration, with a chronic productive cough that has worsened over the past 2 days following a rhinorrhea prodrome.  

Analysis: All three experts agreed that the most likely diagnosis is an acute exacerbation of chronic bronchitis, a manifestation of COPD, based on the patient’s 40‑pack‑year smoking history and chronic productive cough lasting more than 3 months in each of the past 2 years. The panel uniformly found no emergent red‑flag features such as hemoptysis, fever, chest pain, cyanosis, altered mental status, or signs of respiratory failure, supporting outpatient management. Consensus was reached on the need for chest imaging to exclude pneumonia, pulse‑oximetry to assess oxygenation, and spirometry to confirm airflow limitation. Minor points of divergence included Expert A’s suggestion to consider testing for alpha‑1 antitrypsin deficiency despite a low pre‑test probability, and slight variation in the emphasis on when to initiate oral corticosteroids or antibiotics; however, all agreed that antibiotics are reserved for purulent sputum or systemic signs and steroids are considered for moderate‑to‑severe exacerbations.  

Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Measurement of vital signs (blood pressure, heart rate, respiratory rate, temperature), pulse‑oximetry, chest radiograph, spirometry (post‑bronchodilator if possible), review of influenza and COVID‑19 testing as indicated, complete blood count if infection is suspected, and assessment of vaccination status (influenza, pneumococcal).  

Conclusion: Acute exacerbation of chronic bronchitis (COPD exacerbation) requiring non‑emergent, outpatient care.  

Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care  
Subclinical specialization: Pulmonology  

Recommendations: Initiate short‑acting bronchodilator therapy (e.g., albuterol inhaler) for symptom relief; consider a short course of oral corticosteroids if the exacerbation is judged moderate to severe based on symptom burden and oxygen saturation; prescribe antibiotics only if sputum becomes purulent or if systemic signs of bacterial infection develop. Provide intensive smoking‑cessation counseling and offer pharmacologic aids (nicotine replacement, varenicline, or bupropion) together with referral to a cessation program. Verify and update influenza vaccination annually and pneumococcal vaccination according to current guidelines. Arrange a low‑dose CT scan for lung‑cancer screening in accordance with USPSTF criteria (≥30 pack‑year history, age 50‑80, current smoker). Refer the patient to pulmonology for comprehensive COPD evaluation, optimization of inhaler regimen, and enrollment in pulmonary rehabilitation. Screen for common comorbidities such as heart failure, gastro‑esophageal reflux disease, and cor pulmonale, especially if symptoms persist despite initial therapy. Document occupational and environmental exposures that could aggravate airway disease. Consider ordering an alpha‑1 antitrypsin level only if there is a family history, early‑onset disease, or unexplained severe airflow limitation; otherwise, it is not routinely indicated. Schedule a follow‑up visit within 1‑2 weeks to reassess symptoms, oxygen saturation, and response to treatment, and provide clear instructions to return urgently if any red‑flag signs develop.  

Notes: The patient’s repeated winter‑time exacerbations suggest a viral trigger; ensure timely influenza vaccination and counsel on hand hygiene and avoidance of respiratory infections.

Age: 5 years
Sex: Male
Complaint: Itchy erythematous papules on the forearms and lower legs that appeared after an afternoon of outdoor play

Analysis: The presentation of multiple small (3‑5 mm) pruritic papules with central puncta on exposed extremities in a child who was outdoors is classic for papular urticaria caused by arthropod bites. All three experts agreed on this primary diagnosis and on the absence of red‑flag features such as fever, rapid spread of erythema, lymphangitis, systemic allergic reactions, or signs of vector‑borne disease. Consensus also identified supportive care with antihistamines and low‑potency topical steroids as appropriate first‑line management. Divergence arose in the differential diagnosis list: Experts A and B initially omitted bacterial skin infections, whereas Expert C and later Expert B added folliculitis and early cellulitis as possible mimics. This outlier was addressed by acknowledging that, although the current lesions lack warmth, tenderness, purulence, or systemic signs, early bacterial infection can resemble insect‑bite papules and should be kept in mind if the clinical picture evolves. Additional considerations highlighted in the rounds include contact dermatitis (especially if linear streaks or vesicles develop), scabies (less likely given distribution and lack of burrows), viral exanthems (unlikely without fever), and geographic/seasonal influences on vector‑borne disease risk.

Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Visual inspection of the skin; dermatoscopic examination may be useful for confirming central puncta but is not required. No laboratory tests are indicated unless red‑flag features develop (e.g., CBC, wound culture, or serology for tick‑borne illness).

Conclusion: Papular urticaria secondary to insect (mosquito/flea) bites.

Emergency type: Self-care appropriate
Subclinical specialization: Pediatrics

Recommendations: Initiate oral second‑generation antihistamine (e.g., cetirizine 5‑10 mg once daily) for itch control and apply low‑potency topical corticosteroid (hydrocortisone 1 %) to individual lesions twice daily. Advise the caregiver to keep the child’s nails short, discourage scratching, and use gentle skin cleansing with mild soap and water. Monitor for any increase in redness, warmth, swelling, pain, purulent discharge, fever, or regional lymphadenopathy, which would suggest secondary bacterial infection and warrant prompt medical evaluation and possible antibiotics. Educate the caregiver to seek care immediately if any red‑flag signs appear, if lesions spread rapidly, or if systemic symptoms develop. Counsel on preventive measures: apply EPA‑registered insect repellent (DEET or picaridin) before outdoor activities, dress the child in long sleeves and pants, eliminate standing water and tall grass around the home, use window and door screens, treat pets for fleas and ticks, and consider community or yard insect‑control programs. Review the child’s vaccination status and recent illnesses to exclude viral mimics; if fever or systemic signs arise, reassess for viral exanthem or tick‑borne disease based on geographic exposure. Maintain vigilance for contact dermatitis by observing for linear streaks or vesicles, and for scabies by checking for burrows in interdigital spaces; these conditions would require specific therapy. If lesions persist beyond two weeks, become atypical, or show signs of infection, arrange a dermatology referral.

Notes: The inclusion of folliculitis and early cellulitis in the differential reflects an outlier‑driven safety consideration; caregivers should be instructed that the current appearance is consistent with insect bites but that any change in lesion character warrants re‑evaluation.

Age: 77 years  
Sex: Male  
Complaint: Burning and aching right‑sided chest pain for 5 days followed by erythema, maculopapular rash, and progression to clear vesicles, pustules, ulceration and crusting; associated headache and malaise.  

Analysis: All three experts unanimously identified the presentation as classic herpes zoster involving a right thoracic dermatome, noting the typical dermatomal pain preceding a vesicular rash that evolves through maculopapular, vesicular, pustular, ulcerative and crusting stages. Consensus was reached that emergent evaluation is not required in the absence of red‑flag findings such as ophthalmic involvement, disseminated rash, severe uncontrolled pain, signs of bacterial superinfection, immunosuppression, or neurological deficits. Dermatology was agreed upon as the preferred specialty for management, with primary care acceptable if dermatology is unavailable; Infectious Disease consultation was suggested only for complicated or immunocompromised cases. Early oral antiviral therapy (valacyclovir 1 g three times daily for 7 days) with renal dose adjustment, and multimodal pain control were endorsed by all. Routine virologic testing was deemed unnecessary for classic cases. The experts differed on a few points: Expert C highlighted the need for a standardized pain‑severity assessment, evaluation for motor involvement or zoster paresis, consideration of corticosteroids in select severe cases, and explicit patient education on contagion; Expert C also mentioned a possible need for emergent assessment to rule out early complications despite the lack of red flags, and suggested Infectious Disease as a primary specialty, which the majority did not adopt.  

Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Clinical examination of the rash and neurologic assessment, serum creatinine for estimated glomerular filtration rate to guide antiviral dosing, complete blood count if bacterial superinfection is suspected, optional PCR or direct fluorescent antibody testing of vesicle fluid only for atypical or immunocompromised presentations, and visual inspection for Hutchinson’s sign to exclude ophthalmic involvement.  

Conclusion: The patient has herpes zoster affecting a thoracic dermatome and requires prompt, non‑emergent outpatient management with antiviral therapy, pain control, and comprehensive assessment of risk factors and complications.  

Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care  
Subclinical specialization: Dermatology  

Recommendations: Initiate oral valacyclovir 1 g three times daily for 7 days as soon as possible, adjusting to 1 g once daily if creatinine clearance is below 30 mL/min; alternative regimens include acyclovir 800 mg five times daily or famciclovir 500 mg three times daily with similar renal adjustments. Provide multimodal analgesia beginning with acetaminophen or NSAIDs for mild pain, adding gabapentin or pregabalin for moderate to severe neuropathic pain, and consider topical lidocaine patches for localized relief; short‑course opioids may be used for breakthrough pain. Assess pain severity using a numeric rating scale to guide escalation, and evaluate for motor weakness or focal neurological deficits. Counsel the patient on the low risk of contagion, emphasizing hand hygiene, covering lesions, and avoiding contact with varicella‑naïve individuals. Review varicella‑zoster vaccination status and offer Shingrix if the patient is unvaccinated after the acute episode. Screen for immunocompromising conditions (malignancy, HIV, immunosuppressive therapy), obtain renal function labs for dosing, and review comorbidities such as diabetes or chronic kidney disease. Conduct a medication review for potential interactions with antivirals or analgesics, and note any drug allergies, especially to acyclovir/valacyclovir or NSAIDs. Monitor the rash daily for signs of secondary bacterial infection (purulent discharge, increasing erythema, fever) and arrange a follow‑up visit in 1–2 weeks to assess rash resolution and early signs of post‑herpetic neuralgia. Document any prior episodes of herpes zoster or post‑herpetic neuralgia, and consider a brief trial of low‑dose corticosteroids only if pain is severe and inflammation is pronounced, after weighing risks and benefits. Address social determinants that may affect medication access or ability to attend follow‑up, and provide written education on the importance of early antiviral therapy, signs of complications, and strategies to manage pain.  

Notes: Ensure clear documentation of the assessment, treatment plan, and patient education; coordinate care with primary care or infectious disease if immunosuppression or atypical features emerge.

Sex: Female  
Complaint: Six‑month history of bilateral milky nipple discharge, secondary amenorrhea, progressive frontal/headaches, unintentional weight gain, lethargy, decreased libido, and difficulty conceiving.  

Analysis: The markedly elevated serum prolactin (500 µg/L) together with a sellar mass measuring 1.1 × 1.6 × 2.1 cm on contrast‑enhanced MRI, normal TSH, and the clinical triad of galactorrhea, amenorrhea, and headaches is classic for a prolactin‑secreting pituitary macroadenoma (macroprolactinoma). All three experts concur that the lesion is not compressing the optic chiasm and therefore does not constitute an immediate neurosurgical emergency, but prompt endocrinology evaluation and dopamine‑agonist therapy are indicated. Consensus also emphasizes the need for a full pituitary hormonal assessment, visual‑field testing, and serial imaging to monitor response. A point of divergence arose from Expert C, who raised the possibility of a laboratory “hook effect” or macroprolactinemia and recommended a repeat prolactin measurement with sample dilution; this outlier view is noted for inclusion in the work‑up.  

Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Contrast‑enhanced MRI of the brain (baseline already obtained), formal visual‑field perimetry, comprehensive pituitary hormone panel (prolactin repeat with dilution, TSH, free T4, ACTH, cortisol, LH, FSH, estradiol, IGF‑1), basic metabolic panel with renal function, serum electrolytes, blood pressure measurement, bone mineral density assessment (DEXA), depression screening (e.g., PHQ‑9), and routine follow‑up labs to monitor therapy.  

Conclusion: The patient has a prolactin‑secreting pituitary macroadenoma (macroprolactinoma) causing hyperprolactinemia, galactorrhea, amenorrhea, and headaches. The condition is non‑emergent but requires timely medical management and multidisciplinary follow‑up.  

Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care  
Subclinical specialization: Endocrinology  

Recommendations: Initiate dopamine‑agonist therapy with cabergoline, starting at a low dose and titrating to achieve normalization of prolactin and tumor shrinkage; counsel the patient on the importance of strict adherence and potential side‑effects. Arrange expedited referral to an endocrinologist for medication management, monitoring of prolactin levels, and repeat MRI in 6–12 months to assess tumor response. Perform formal visual‑field testing now and repeat if symptoms evolve. Order a full pituitary hormone panel to detect co‑secretion or hypopituitarism and repeat the prolactin assay using serial dilutions to exclude a hook effect or macroprolactin interference. Evaluate bone health with DEXA scanning and advise adequate calcium and vitamin D intake; consider bisphosphonate therapy if osteopenia/osteoporosis is identified. Screen for depression with a validated questionnaire and refer for counseling or psychiatric care as needed. Monitor blood pressure and treat persistent hypertension according to standard guidelines. Provide education on red‑flag signs of pituitary apoplexy (sudden severe headache, visual loss, nausea, vomiting) and instruct the patient to seek immediate medical attention if they occur. Coordinate with reproductive endocrinology to discuss timing of conception, the possibility of continuing cabergoline during pregnancy, and strategies for fertility optimization once prolactin levels are controlled. Ensure the patient understands the need for regular follow‑up appointments, laboratory testing, and imaging to track disease course.  

Notes: The patient’s mild hypertension, weight gain, and depressive symptoms warrant concurrent management alongside endocrine therapy. Ongoing assessment of cortisol and adrenal function is advisable given the headache progression and weight changes.

winner_protocol:
Age: 44  
Sex: Female  
Complaint: Progressive nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, abdominal pain with refractory hypotension, electrolyte abnormalities, and altered mental status in the setting of known Addison disease.  

Analysis: All three experts unanimously diagnosed an acute primary adrenal (Addisonian) crisis precipitated by viral gastroenteritis causing loss of oral glucocorticoid and mineralocorticoid absorption. The convergence highlights refractory hypotension, profound hyponatremia (Na 118), severe hyperkalemia (K 6.4) with ECG changes (peaked T waves, prolonged PR), hypoglycemia (glucose 52), acute kidney injury, low random cortisol (1.2 µg/dL), and characteristic hyperpigmentation as definitive red‑flags. Consensus management includes immediate high‑dose IV hydrocortisone, aggressive isotonic saline with dextrose, rapid correction of hyperkalemia, cardiac monitoring, and vasopressor support if needed, with endocrinology leading ongoing care. Points of divergence: Expert A mentioned the theoretical use of a parenteral mineralocorticoid, whereas Experts B and C emphasized that fludrocortisone is oral and that high‑dose hydrocortisone provides sufficient mineralocorticoid activity. Expert B placed greater emphasis on early abdominal imaging to rule out adrenal hemorrhage, while Expert C added the need to consider adrenal vein thrombosis, possible bacterial superinfection requiring empiric antibiotics, and detailed patient education on sick‑day rules. Expert C also noted that the questionnaire missed these aspects, prompting additional considerations.  

Required diagnostic equipment/tests: 12‑lead ECG; bedside cardiac telemetry; point‑of‑care glucose; serum electrolytes, renal panel, cortisol, ACTH; arterial blood gas and lactate; serum osmolality; urine output measurement; blood cultures; stool studies; abdominal contrast‑enhanced CT (if adrenal hemorrhage or thrombosis suspected); chest radiograph if respiratory infection considered.  

Conclusion: The patient is experiencing a life‑threatening primary adrenal crisis that requires immediate emergent intervention and coordinated endocrine follow‑up.  

Emergency type: Requires emergent care  
Subclinical specialization: Endocrinology  

Recommendations: Initiate IV hydrocortisone 100 mg bolus followed by 200 mg/24 h either as continuous infusion or 50 mg IV every 6 hours. Begin rapid isotonic saline boluses of 1‑2 L, repeat as needed, and incorporate dextrose (e.g., 5 % dextrose in saline) to address hypoglycemia and prevent further glucose decline. Administer 10 mL of 10 % calcium gluconate IV for cardiac membrane stabilization, then give regular insulin 10 U IV with 25 g dextrose to shift potassium intracellularly; consider additional potassium‑binding agents or emergent dialysis if potassium remains >6.5 mEq/L despite these measures. Maintain continuous cardiac telemetry and obtain serial ECGs to monitor for resolution of hyperkalemic changes. Correct serum sodium cautiously, limiting rise to no more than 8‑10 mEq/L in any 24‑hour period to avoid osmotic demyelination. Monitor urine output hourly, serum lactate, arterial pH, and repeat electrolytes every 2‑4 hours until stable. If hypotension persists after 1‑2 L fluid and steroid administration, start norepinephrine infusion, titrating to maintain MAP ≥ 65 mmHg. Obtain blood cultures and stool studies promptly; if clinical suspicion for bacterial superinfection exists, initiate empiric broad‑spectrum antibiotics after cultures are drawn. Perform abdominal CT with contrast if shock is disproportionate to volume status, if flank or abdominal pain develops, or if adrenal hemorrhage or adrenal vein thrombosis is suspected. Hold oral fludrocortisone until the patient can tolerate enteral intake; rely on the mineralocorticoid effect of high‑dose hydrocortisone in the interim. Review all current medications for interactions that may alter steroid metabolism. Once stabilized, arrange endocrinology follow‑up for long‑term management, repeat cortisol/ACTH testing, and education. Provide comprehensive patient education on sick‑day rules, emphasizing the need for stress‑dose steroids during illness, the availability of injectable hydrocortisone for emergencies, and instructions on when to seek immediate medical care.  

Notes: Ensure rapid coordination between emergency, intensive care, and endocrinology teams. Document all interventions and monitor for potential complications such as osmotic demyelination, arrhythmias, refractory shock, and adrenal hemorrhage.

Age: 55
Sex: Male
Complaint: Rapidly worsening pain, swelling, and redness of the right lower leg with systemic toxicity following a minor abrasion.

Analysis: The patient presents with classic features of necrotizing fasciitis—including severe pain out of proportion to exam, tense dusky erythema, hemorrhagic bullae, crepitus, systemic signs of sepsis, a LRINEC score of 10, and CT evidence of gas tracking along fascial planes—combined with poorly controlled diabetes and acute kidney injury. All three experts converged on the diagnosis of necrotizing fasciitis and agreed that emergent surgical debridement and broad‑spectrum intravenous antibiotics are mandatory, with General Surgery as the primary specialty responsible for definitive care. Consensus differed in the scope of multidisciplinary involvement: Expert A limited the consult to General Surgery alone, whereas Experts B and C emphasized early involvement of Emergency Medicine for stabilization, Infectious Disease for antimicrobial optimization, Critical Care for ICU management of septic shock, Nephrology for renal dosing adjustments, and Endocrinology for tight glycemic control. The unified plan therefore incorporates both the core surgical imperative and the broader multidisciplinary support highlighted by the majority of experts.

Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Computed tomography of the affected leg (already obtained), bedside ultrasound or MRI if diagnostic uncertainty persisted, complete blood count, comprehensive metabolic panel, serum lactate, C‑reactive protein, coagulation profile, blood cultures prior to antibiotics, type‑and‑crossmatch, arterial blood gas, and serial monitoring of renal function and electrolytes.

Conclusion: Necrotizing fasciitis of the right lower leg requiring emergent operative debridement.

Emergency type: Requires emergent care
Subclinical specialization: General Surgery

Recommendations: Activate the surgical “code” and transport the patient immediately to the operating room for wide‑area fascial exploration and debridement; obtain a pre‑operative type‑and‑crossmatch in anticipation of possible massive blood loss. Initiate empiric broad‑spectrum antibiotics covering gram‑positive (including MRSA), gram‑negative, and anaerobic organisms—e.g., vancomycin plus piperacillin‑tazobactam or a carbapenem—adjusted for the current creatinine of 2.4 mg/dL. Begin aggressive fluid resuscitation with 30 mL/kg isotonic crystalloid, followed by vasopressor support (norepinephrine) to maintain MAP > 65 mm Hg. Implement an insulin infusion to target glucose 140–180 mg/dL, recognizing that hyperglycemia worsens infection and impairs wound healing. Provide tetanus prophylaxis given the contaminated wound. Continuously monitor for compartment syndrome by clinical exam and, if indicated, compartment pressure measurements. Serially assess lactate, renal function, electrolytes, and coagulation parameters to detect evolving tissue hypoperfusion, acute kidney injury progression, or disseminated intravascular coagulation. Engage Infectious Disease for antimicrobial stewardship, Critical Care for ongoing sepsis management, Nephrology for renal‑adjusted dosing and potential renal replacement therapy, and Endocrinology for diabetes optimization. Consider analgesia with multimodal agents and procedural sedation as needed for painful debridement. Post‑operatively admit the patient to the ICU for hemodynamic monitoring, repeat debridement as dictated by wound status, and early involvement of wound‑care specialists. Evaluate peripheral arterial disease, which may affect healing, and plan for vascular assessment if perfusion concerns arise.

Notes: The prior prescription of oral cephalexin was insufficient for this fulminant infection and underscores the need for rapid escalation to intravenous broad‑spectrum therapy. The presence of hyponatremia and renal impairment mandates careful fluid and drug dosing. Ongoing multidisciplinary coordination is essential to address the complex metabolic, infectious, and surgical challenges presented by this case.

Age: 20 years  
Sex: Male  
Complaint: Itchy, peeling skin between the third and fourth interdigital web spaces of both feet for 2 weeks; no pain, swelling, or spread beyond the webs; normal toenails.  

Analysis: The clinical picture—bilateral interdigital maceration, peeling, and mild erythema in a young athlete with daily communal shower use—is classic for interdigital tinea pedis caused by dermatophytes. All three experts agreed on this primary diagnosis and on the non‑urgent nature of the condition. Consensus also identified the need for foot‑drying hygiene, topical allylamine therapy, and referral only if refractory or complicated. Divergence arose regarding the initial managing specialty: Expert A emphasized dermatology as the primary point of care, whereas Experts B and C considered primary‑care management sufficient before specialist referral. All experts concurred on red‑flag features that would prompt urgent reassessment and on the utility of KOH preparation, fungal culture, and Wood’s lamp to rule out mimickers such as erythrasma, candida intertrigo, scabies, or psoriasis.  

Required diagnostic equipment/tests: KOH preparation of skin scrapings; fungal culture if KOH negative but suspicion remains; Wood’s lamp examination to detect erythrasma (coral‑red fluorescence); optional dermoscopy or PCR in ambiguous cases.  

Conclusion: Interdigital tinea pedis (athlete’s foot) due to dermatophyte infection.  

Emergency type: Self-care appropriate  
Subclinical specialization: Dermatology  

Recommendations: Initiate topical allylamine therapy (e.g., terbinafine 1 % cream) applied twice daily to the affected webs for 2–4 weeks, as allylamines have higher cure rates than azoles. Reinforce foot‑hygiene measures: dry feet thoroughly after showers, especially between toes; change socks at least daily; wear moisture‑wicking, breathable footwear; rotate shoes every 2–3 days and apply antifungal powder to shoes; use shower shoes in communal facilities. Advise the patient to avoid walking barefoot in shared showers and locker rooms. Monitor for red‑flag signs—pain, swelling, warmth, fever, rapid spread, fissuring, involvement of soles or nails, or secondary bacterial infection—and seek prompt medical review if they appear. If no clinical improvement after 2 weeks of appropriate topical therapy, if atypical features develop (e.g., vesicles, extensive erythema, nail changes), or if recurrence occurs, arrange referral to dermatology for possible oral antifungal therapy or further investigation. In cases of recurrent, extensive, or treatment‑resistant infection, screen for underlying systemic risk factors such as diabetes, HIV, or other immunosuppressive conditions despite the patient’s negative history.  

Notes: The patient’s normal toenails indicate no current onychomycosis; however, progression to nail involvement is a known complication of untreated interdigital tinea pedis. Emphasize education on preventive strategies to reduce re‑exposure in communal shower environments.
